title: Investigating the Effect of Retrieval Context Size on Safety Benchmark Scores

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Zhang et al. (2025) 'RAG LLMs are Not Safer' (NAACL 2025) directly investigated this question across 11 LLMs with over 5,000 harmful prompts, varying the number of retrieved documents and measuring how safety degrades with increasing context. They found that providing more documents makes LLMs more vulnerable, and that even a single safe document can alter a model's risk profile. The core hypothesis of this idea — that longer RAG contexts overwhelm safety filters — is the central finding of that paper. The remaining gap is a finer-grained token-level analysis (512, 2K, 8K, 32K) rather than document-count variation, but the fundamental result is established.

title: Tool for Visualizing Safety Benchmark Coverage Gaps Using Embedding Projections

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: While embedding-based analysis (UMAP, sentence transformers) and safety benchmarks (AILuminate, HELM, TrustLLM) are individually well-established, no published work applies dimensionality reduction visualization specifically to map coverage gaps across safety benchmarks. Coverage-guided testing exists in software testing (MNCOVER for NLP), and 'The Scales of Justitia' surveys safety evaluation comprehensively, but neither produces an interactive visual tool identifying sparse regions in safety benchmark prompt space. The idea combines known techniques in a novel application.

title: Investigating Halo Effects in Safety Scoring: Do High-Quality Responses Get Higher Safety Scores?

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: LLM-as-judge biases are extensively studied. The CALM framework identifies 12 bias types in LLM judges including verbosity bias and style bias. Self-preference bias (arXiv:2410.21819) shows LLMs favor their own outputs. 'Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge' documents style and authority biases. However, these studies focus on general quality evaluation, not specifically on safety scoring. The specific hypothesis that response quality inflates *safety* scores (as opposed to general quality scores) has not been directly tested with paired unsafe-but-quality-varied responses. The safety-specific framing adds novelty to an otherwise well-studied phenomenon.

title: Benchmark for Safety Under Adversarial Few-Shot Examples

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: SG-Bench (NeurIPS 2024) explicitly evaluates safety generalization across prompt types including few-shot demonstrations, with FS-G (benign examples) and FS-H (harmful refusal examples) configurations. 'How Few-shot Demonstrations Affect Prompt-based Defenses Against LLM Jailbreak Attacks' (arXiv:2602.04294, 2026) directly studies how few-shot examples interact with safety defenses. The idea of adversarial few-shot examples as an attack vector is also covered in indirect prompt injection literature. However, the specific framing of constructing a dedicated benchmark of 100 adversarial few-shot compliance demonstrations and comparing against zero-shot baselines across models is a narrower contribution that partially overlaps but is not fully subsumed.

title: Investigating Benchmark Score Variance Due to Prompt Batching

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Research on batch size effects on LLM benchmark accuracy documents 7-10 percentage point differences due to batching (left-padding, floating-point arithmetic differences). 'Efficient but Vulnerable: Benchmarking and Defending LLM Batch Prompting Attack' (arXiv:2503.15551, 2025) addresses batch prompting from a security angle. The general principle that evaluation configuration (including batch size) affects results is established. However, the specific application to safety benchmarks — measuring how batching changes safety verdicts specifically — is not directly studied. The safety-specific angle adds some novelty to an otherwise known methodological concern.

title: Tool for Automated Safety Regression Testing in CI/CD Pipelines

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Multiple mature tools already exist: Promptfoo provides CI/CD integration for LLM security and safety testing with configurable thresholds; DeepEval offers unit testing in CI/CD pipelines with safety metrics; Evidently AI provides LLM testing with GitHub Actions integration; Giskard offers red teaming and safety scanning integrated into development workflows. The idea of a Python package that runs safety probes on model checkpoints in CI/CD with pass/fail signals is essentially what these existing tools already deliver. The space is commercially and open-source saturated.

title: Investigating Whether Safety Benchmarks Are Sensitive to Chat Template Formatting

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Furman (2024) 'Evaluations with Chat Formats' on HuggingFace demonstrated significant uplift in IFEval scores from chat template formatting, establishing that template choice materially affects benchmark results. However, that work focused on instruction-following evaluations, not safety benchmarks specifically. The author explicitly noted the effects 'don't necessarily generalize to all LM evals' and called for extending to safety and other domains. The general principle (templates matter for benchmarks) is established, but the specific safety benchmark application remains untested in published literature.

The correlation between baseline safety and adversarial robustness has been explored in multiple jailbreak benchmarking papers. The specific contribution of computing correlation between baseline safety score and GCG suffix ASR adds incremental value but the components are well-established.

title: Benchmark for Cultural Safety: Harm Definitions Across Cultural Contexts

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: This area has seen substantial recent work. CROSS (2025) provides 1,284 multilingual culturally-grounded queries from 16 countries evaluating cultural norm violations. CASA evaluates cultural and social awareness. The PEREN multilingual testing exercise also addresses cross-cultural safety evaluation. The core proposition — that harm assessment is culturally variable and benchmarks should reflect this — is well-established with multiple published benchmarks already addressing it.

title: Investigating Self-Consistency of Safety Scores Across Repeated Runs

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: This is directly addressed by multiple recent papers. 'Evaluating LLM Safety Under Repeated Inference via Accelerated Prompt Stress Testing' (APST, arXiv:2602.11786, 2026) repeatedly samples identical prompts under controlled conditions to surface latent failure modes and establishes that models with similar benchmark scores have substantially different failure rates under repeated sampling. 'Fine-Tuning Lowers Safety and Disrupts Evaluation Consistency' (arXiv:2506.17209, 2025) compares safety at temperature 0 and 0.7 with 5 repeats. 'Safer or Luckier?' (arXiv:2503.09347, 2025) questions whether single-sample evaluations are representative. The instability of refusal behavior across random seeds and temperatures is now a well-documented finding.

title: Constructing a Minimal Viable Safety Benchmark for Resource-Constrained Evaluators

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: AILuminate itself uses a subset selection approach: 1,200 seed prompts selected from a larger dataset, and the v0.5 Security evaluator uses an improved subset of the v1.0 Safety evaluator. The concept of efficient benchmark subsets that preserve rankings is established in general ML evaluation (e.g., efficient benchmark design, item response theory for benchmarks). However, the specific optimization problem of finding a minimal prompt subset (50-200 items) that maximally preserves model rankings on the full AILuminate benchmark, validated on held-out models, has not been published as a standalone study. The methodological contribution is incremental but the specific deliverable is novel.

'Reasoning Theater' (arXiv:2603.05488, 2026) disentangles model beliefs from CoT. The core idea — that CoT traces reveal misalignment invisible in final outputs — is the central thesis of this entire research program.

title: Replicating Safety Benchmarks Across System Prompt Languages

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Multilingual safety vulnerabilities are well-documented: low-resource languages achieve 80.92% unsafe output rates on ChatGPT; LinguaSafe (arXiv:2508.12733, 2025) benchmarks multilingual safety; 'All Languages Matter' documents cross-lingual safety gaps; code-mixing attacks achieve 90%+ ASR in some cases. 'Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages' (arXiv:2505.17306, 2025) provides mechanistic insights. However, the specific 2x2 design of system-prompt language x user-query language (e.g., English-Chinese, Chinese-English) focusing on the system prompt as the variable has not been systematically studied. Most work varies the user query language, not the system prompt language. This specific angle adds novelty.
